title: A Visit to a Temple in Tamil Nadu
body: During a school trip, Meera visits a large temple complex in Tamil Nadu. She enters through a tall, richly carved gateway called a gopuram, which her guide calls the boundary between the outer world and the sacred space within. Inside the enclosure walls (prakaras) she finds several secondary shrines, one of them dedicated to goddess Parvati. A huge statue of a sacred bull, carved from a single stone, sits in a pavilion facing the main shrine. She then walks through pillared halls (mandapas) towards the innermost chamber, which faces east. Above this chamber rises a massive pyramidal tower. The guide explains that the walls are covered with granite carvings and that the planning of such temples followed the rules of shilpashastra and involved a good deal of geometry.

title: The Taj Mahal and Its Protection
body: In the mid-17th century, Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal at Agra as a mausoleum for his queen Mumtaz Mahal. Its charbagh gardens and large arched doorways are of Persian inspiration, Arabic calligraphy from the Qur'an adorns its walls, and Indian builders added chhatris, lotus designs and marble screens. Craftsmen embedded semi-precious stones into the white marble to create floral inlay. In the 1970s, people noticed that the marble was turning yellowish. The cause was air pollution from local industries that burnt coal and other fossil fuels. After an expert committee made recommendations and a public interest litigation (PIL) was heard in the Supreme Court, a ban was imposed in the mid-1990s to prevent industrial pollution in the area.
